title: 🍉 Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs)
summary:
It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!
The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture!
If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have.
We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.
To get there, we need three things in my opinion:
- Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks
- Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them
- Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders
If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger.
And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more.
It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

Bro, this is actually a huge AMD moment.
Kimi K3 is so massive that it needs 16x B200s across two NVIDIA servers, but it fits inside one 8x MI355X AMD server because AMD gives you much more HBM memory per GPU.
That single AMD node hit:
- 952 tok/s total throughput
- 118 tok/s for a single user
- Nearly 4x the throughput per node of the 16× B200 setup
- Better performance per dollar than both B200 and B300
But the craziest part is that ROCm mostly worked out of the box.
@wafer_ai only had to make a few relatively small fixes. No months of kernel engineering. No custom kernels at all.
Even the slow time-to-first-token problem came down mostly to one attention kernel not loading because Kimi had 12 heads instead of a supported shape. They simply padded 12 to 16, used AMD’s fast existing kernel, and cut cold-prefill time by roughly 2–3x
AMD’s bet on packing more HBM into each server is going to become extremely important as frontier open models keep getting larger.
If AMD keeps improving ROCm and day-one model support, data-center operators will have to seriously consider these GPUs.
The CUDA moat isn’t dead yet, but this definitely puts a big dent in it.

these engineers figured out how to serve Kimi K3 on @AMD MI355X at 952 tok/s/node and 118 tok/s single stream!
this crushes B200 by 3.8x in aggregate throughput/node and 1.3x in single stream decode + beats B300 on performance per dollar (48 vs 33 tok/s/$)

title: 🍉 Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs)
summary:
Exa is now one of the largest indexes in the world.
We serve 80B pages, track 1.4T urls, and are on track to be Google-scale in early 2027.
It's difficult to know the size of indexes, but we estimate Google to be ~1T, Bing to be ~500B, and Yandex ~200B. Brave mentioned in April that they're at 40B.
Most of the web is trash that can hurt AI outputs, so you actually have to crawl way more than you serve and train models to filter out the trash.
In terms of peak QPS, we estimate Bing at roughly 30k/s and Google at ~500k/s.
In our case, because agent traffic often requires large fan-out (deep searches can use dozens of sub-searches) and can be spiky (like when AI labs RL with us), we're already starting to provision for Bing-scale traffic.
Within 2 years, agents will search at many millions per second. They'll also want comprehensiveness over all data, far bigger than any index today. So the retrieval infra required will be larger than Google-scale in both dimensions.

clean_title: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI research and evaluation
summary:
Recently, someone joined @OpenAI to work on "RSI evals"
What does that mean? RSI stands for Recursive Self-Improvement, a term that has become relevant in 2026. RSI refers to a class of AI systems that iteratively improve the mechanisms responsible for producing their own successors, allowing gains in the system to strengthen the process that generates further gains.
Think of it like GPT-5 helping people to release GPT-6. Of course, you want to evaluate how much the model is helping towards creating its own successor;
- How much speedup is gained on pre-training?
- How much speedup is gained on post-training?
- etc.
It's the main reason why Karpathy joined @AnthropicAI as well: to leverage Claude to speed up pre-training research
Modern papers discuss self-modifying agents, automated AI research, executable feedback, and repeated training or search loops, etc.
Learn more here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HO49fsgW4AAAk7g.jpg
Quoting @cooperjsaye
I recently joined @OpenAI in San Francisco, where I’ll be working on RSI evals.
I’m excited by AI’s potential to accelerate AI research itself, and I’m looking forward to learning from some very talented people!
clean_summary:
Recently, someone joined @OpenAI to work on RSI evals. RSI, or Recursive Self-Improvement, refers to AI systems that iteratively enhance the mechanisms responsible for creating their own successors, enabling progress to accelerate itself. This concept is gaining relevance in 2026, with applications like GPT-5 helping develop GPT-6, and is a key focus in modern AI research involving self-modifying agents, automated AI development, executable feedback, and repeated training or search loops.

The work aims to evaluate how much models contribute to speeding up pre-training and post-training processes, reflecting AI's potential to accelerate its own progress. Karpathy's move to @AnthropicAI to leverage Claude for faster pre-training research exemplifies this trend. More information can be found in papers and benchmarks on RSI at Papers with Code.

title: 🍉 Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs)
summary:
Some people are surprised that APIs (aka what Anthropic, OpenAI, and others provide) are treated differently than open weights in the new AI model framework.
I'm not surprised at all, and it's actually very good policy. Let me explain:
Model weights, APIs, and apps are three very different layers of the stack. Treating them the same would be a recipe for bad regulation.
Think about how we handle cars. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Nobody asks a steel mill to guarantee that nothing dangerous will ever be built with its steel. Obligations sit with the carmaker and rules of the road with the driver, because that's where risk becomes real and where someone can actually act on it.
Model weights are the steel of AI. They're raw research output, closer to science than product: no user, no interface, no deployment. They don't do anything on their own. And because everything else is built on top of them, this is the layer where regulation does the most damage. Restrict weights and you slow down all progress downstream, and you prevent countless positive use cases from ever emerging: the lab fine-tuning an open model for rare diseases, the startup serving a language big providers ignore, the safety researchers who can only audit models because the weights are open. You don't reduce risk, you just kill open source and concentrate power in a few big labs.
APIs are the middle layer, the parts and engine suppliers of AI: a commercial service where a provider serves a model at scale. Here you have a business relationship, terms of service, the ability to monitor for abuse. It makes sense to expect transparency, security standards, and accountability from providers at this layer, because they can actually enforce things.
Apps are the car on the road: where AI meets the real world. A medical assistant, a hiring tool, a companion for kids, a financial advisor. This is where concrete harm can happen, and conveniently, it's where we already have decades of regulation. Health, finance, employment, consumer protection. An AI hiring tool should comply with employment law whether it's powered by an open model, an API, or a spreadsheet.
The principle is simple: regulate at the layer where risk actually materializes and where actors can act on it. Push obligations to the deployment layer, keep the research layer open. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Well done @realDonaldTrump @DavidSacks @mkratsios47!

* Has potential for high real world impact
* Clearly used extensively at frontier labs
* Almost no empirical literature exists
* More accessible on academic compute

title: 🍉 Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs)
summary:
I sent this to my extended family today. You should too, if you haven't yet.
---
By the way, family, I think we’re entering the “start buying hand sanitizer” phase of a massive wave of ai powered hacks. You used to be safer because it wasn’t worth a human’s time to hack *you specifically,* but that isn’t true anymore.
You should:
- set up a password manager
- make sure you’re not using the same password on multiple accounts, or slight variations on the same password, unless you’re ok with those accounts getting hacked
- make sure you’re using secure multifactor authentication (NOT sms!)
- be skeptical of phone calls and emails, even if they look like they’re coming from people you know and even if you recognize the voice on the phone. Hackers can clone someone’s voice very easily
- update your phone and computer every time you’re prompted to
- it used to be that fishing emails were deliberately unrealistic so that they would only get the most gullible people. This isn’t true anymore. You will get increasingly realistic fishing emails and phone calls with what look like videos of people you know.
Setting this up will probably take a few hours of boring paperwork, but it’s worth it.
It used to be that you just had to be “faster than the other guy, not faster than the bear”. Not anymore. Fully automated hacks are starting and they’ve caused 100s of millions of dollars of damage and losses already, maybe more. It’s going to ramp up from here.

clean_title: 11B end-to-end real-time streaming voice model for conversational AI
summary:
割り込みできる！すげー
会話型 AI 向けの 11B エンドツーエンドのリアルタイム音声フルデュプレックスモデルで、ストリーミング音声理解と音声生成を共同で実行します。
従来のカスケードスタック (ASR → LLM → TTS) とは異なり、このモデルは、1 つの統合アーキテクチャでフルデュプレックス、リアルタイム、シームレスな音声インタラクションを実現し、複数のモデルや API ハンドオフの必要性を排除し、エンドツーエンドのレイテンシを削減します。オープンで堅牢、かつ非常に自然な会話機能を提供することで、新たなベンチマークを確立します。
さらに、ツール実行中に自然な会話の流れを維持しながらツール呼び出しをサポートする初のオープンフルデュプレックスモデルです。各ツールに対して、LLM がツール呼び出しと応答をトリガーするテキストを生成するとすぐにエージェントによって話される特定の「保留」メッセージを定義できます！
clean_summary: Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs) introduces a full-duplex, real-time, streaming speech model designed for conversational AI. Unlike traditional cascaded stacks (ASR → LLM → TTS), this integrated architecture enables seamless, low-latency voice interactions without the need for multiple models or API handoffs, providing natural and robust conversations. It also supports tool calls within ongoing dialogue, allowing the language model to trigger tool interactions and generate specific 'hold' messages for speech output immediately after tool responses.

clean_summary: Abubakar Abid announces the release of BTL-4 35B, a frontier agentic reasoning model, and Macaw 2.7B, an on-device Mac agent. Both are open weights and available now. BTL-4 achieves 73.5% on BFCL v4 (AST), surpassing the base model by 4.3 points, and scores 78.4% verified on SWE-bench. It also reaches 66.1% on LiveCodeBench v6, with a full 442-problem window and a native context of 262K tokens, which improves its performance by 5.2 points when increased. Macaw 2.7B is designed as the assistant a Mac should have shipped with, supporting 97 verified macOS tools, reading screen and documents locally without cloud or vision models, and running efficiently on an M2. It is 1.5 GB on disk, uses about 2 GB RAM, and responds in around 2 seconds. Both models support vLLM and MLX from day one, with open weights deployable anywhere.

title: 🍉 Abubakar Abid (@abidlabs)
summary:
1.59GB. That is the entire agent.
Liquid shipped LFM2.5-2.6B yesterday. The Q4_0 GGUF is 1.59GB, 128K context, pre-trained on roughly 34T tokens. Their claim: it beats Qwen3.5-9B on ToolSandbox, 77.83 to 76.44, at a quarter of the size.
I pointed my own tool-calling harness at it instead of reading the chart. Twenty tasks, seven tools, everything local through llama.cpp:
llama-cli -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF
metric LFM2.5-2.6B my usual 8B
correct tool picked 17 / 20 18 / 20
valid JSON args 20 / 20 19 / 20
tok/s 61.4 22.8
peak RSS 2.31 GB 6.04 GB
It lost one task on tool choice and won outright on argument formatting, which is the part that actually breaks agent loops at 2am.
The honest tradeoff: it plans two steps well and four steps badly. Give it a chain longer than three calls and it starts re-calling the tool it already has an answer from. For a phone-resident agent doing short bounded jobs, fine. For a research loop, no.
Marginal cost per run is zero. That is the number people will care about in six months.
